title: Von Neumann Architecture
learningObjective: Understand the stored-program concept where instructions and data share a unified memory space and bus, and diagnose the resulting Von Neumann Bottleneck.
technicalDefinition: A stored-program computer architecture (formalized in the 1945 EDVAC draft report) consisting of a Processing Unit, Control Unit, unified Memory storing both instructions and data, and I/O interfaces.
engineeringExplanation: Because instructions and program data reside in the same addressable RAM and traverse the same memory bus, the CPU cannot fetch an instruction word and read or write a data operand across that unified bus in the same clock cycle without arbitration or caching. In modern CPUs, external DRAM remains unified Von Neumann storage, while on-die caches apply Modified Harvard splits (L1i / L1d) to relieve this bottleneck.
generalVsVendorNote: General principle: stored-program unified RAM model applies across x86, ARM, and RISC-V systems, while commercial implementations add split L1 caches and wide DRAM channels to hide bus contention. TIAN-ISA v1 separates Instruction Memory and Data Memory (Modified Harvard) so beginners cannot accidentally overwrite instructions via STORE.

title: Harvard & Modified Harvard Architecture
learningObjective: Explain why separating instruction and data pathways doubles front-end fetch/data concurrency and how modern CPUs adopt Modified Harvard L1 caches.
technicalDefinition: A computer architecture featuring physically or logically separate storage memories and signal buses for instructions versus data, enabling simultaneous instruction fetch and data access.
engineeringExplanation: Pure Harvard designs (common in DSPs and microcontrollers) prevent accidental code corruption and double memory bandwidth by reading instructions on Bus A while reading or writing operands on Bus B. General-purpose desktop and server CPUs adopt a Modified Harvard hierarchy: unified DRAM plus L3 and L2 caches feed split L1 caches (L1i for fetch, L1d for load/store), delivering simultaneous fetch and load concurrency every cycle without sacrificing programmable flexibility.
generalVsVendorNote: General Modified Harvard split at L1 is standard across commercial high-performance cores; exact L1 capacity and port counts vary by microarchitecture. Directly matches TIAN-ISA v1's separate InstructionMemory[0..255] and DataMemory[0..255].

title: RISC and CISC Design Philosophies
learningObjective: Compare Reduced Instruction Set Computer (RISC) and Complex Instruction Set Computer (CISC) trade-offs in decoding complexity, code density, and micro-op translation.
technicalDefinition: Two contrasting ISA philosophies: RISC favors fixed-width, regular-format, load-store instructions executing in simple cycles, whereas CISC favors variable-length, memory-capable multi-step instructions maximizing code compactness.
engineeringExplanation: Historically, CISC minimized assembly instruction count when RAM was scarce, requiring complex microcode sequencers and multi-byte decoders. RISC emphasized uniform register-to-register ALU instructions with explicit LOAD/STORE memory separation, simplifying pipelining. Modern commercial CISC processors bridge this gap internally by decoding variable-length instructions into fixed-format internal micro-operations (uops), whereas RISC architectures remain load-store at the ISA boundary while incorporating rich extensions.
generalVsVendorNote: TIAN-ISA v1 models a clean RISC-inspired load-store style for arithmetic (ADD R3, R1, R2 operates solely on registers while STORE/LOAD [addr] touch memory), keeping decode visuals transparent without claiming ARM, RISC-V, or x86 binary compatibility.

title: Instruction Set Architecture (ISA)
learningObjective: Distinguish the Instruction Set Architecture (hardware/software contract) from physical microarchitecture (implementation).
technicalDefinition: The formal programmer-visible specification defining supported opcodes, data types, architectural registers, memory addressing modes, status flags, and exception semantics.
engineeringExplanation: The ISA forms the abstraction boundary decoupling compiler and software ecosystems from evolving silicon designs. Two chips implementing the same ISA can exhibit vastly different microarchitectures—differing cache sizes, pipeline depths, and out-of-order execution widths—yet execute identical binaries. Microarchitectural techniques such as register renaming map small architectural register sets onto much larger physical SRAM files inside real silicon.
generalVsVendorNote: TIANEDGE explicitly implements TIAN-ISA v1 as an educational ISA contract (16 mnemonics, R0-R7, Z/N/C/V flags) rather than any proprietary vendor ISA.

title: CPU Pipelining & Hazards
learningObjective: Understand how overlapping instruction stages raises throughput (IPC -> 1) without reducing single-instruction latency, and identify structural, data, and control hazards.
technicalDefinition: A temporal parallelization technique that divides instruction processing into independent clocked stages separated by pipeline registers (flip-flops), allowing multiple instructions to occupy successive stages simultaneously.
engineeringExplanation: Instead of waiting 6 cycles before starting Instruction 2, a 5- or 6-stage hardware pipeline starts Instruction 2 on Cycle 2 while Instruction 1 moves into Decode. Ideal speedup scales with pipeline depth, limited by latch overhead, clock skew, and three hazards: Structural hazards (resource contention, solved by splitting L1i/L1d), Data hazards (RAW dependencies like ADD R3, R1, R2 followed by STORE R3, 100, solved via forwarding/bypass paths or stalls), and Control hazards (branches altering PC).
generalVsVendorNote: TIANEDGE's CPU Simulator intentionally executes one instruction sequentially across 6 stages (CPI = 6) for single-instruction visual clarity, whereas hardware pipelines overlap instructions to approach CPI = 1.

title: Branch Prediction & Speculation
learningObjective: Explain why conditional branches (JZ, JNZ) threaten deep pipelines and how hardware predictors minimize flush penalties.
technicalDefinition: Hardware front-end mechanisms (Branch Target Buffers, dynamic 2-bit saturating counters, history-based predictors) that predict branch direction and target address before execution resolves FLAGS.
engineeringExplanation: In deep pipelines spanning 10 to 20+ stages in commercial cores, waiting until EXECUTE to learn whether JNZ LOOP jumps wastes dozens of execution slots per branch. Branch predictors guess taken or not-taken during FETCH and speculatively execute down the predicted path; on misprediction, uncommitted instructions are flushed and PC redirects to the true target.
generalVsVendorNote: TIAN-ISA v1 resolves JZ/JNZ deterministically in EXECUTE without speculative fetch since the simulator is non-pipelined; commercial CPUs deploy multi-table TAGE or perceptron predictors.

title: Cache Hierarchy & Locality
learningObjective: Analyze why CPUs combine small fast SRAM (Register File -> L1 -> L2 -> L3) with large slower DRAM using temporal and spatial locality.
technicalDefinition: A multi-level memory pyramid trading capacity for ultra-low access latency and energy efficiency, parameterized by Average Memory Access Time (AMAT).
engineeringExplanation: Because transistor switching speed scaled far faster than off-die DRAM latency (the Memory Wall), a single main memory access costs hundreds of processor cycles. Caching keeps recently used values (temporal locality) and adjacent memory words fetched in cache lines (spatial locality) close to the ALU in multi-level SRAM arrays.
generalVsVendorNote: Exact L1/L2/L3 sizes, associativity, and inclusion policies vary across processor families, while the SRAM-to-DRAM latency pyramid and AMAT relationship hold universally.

title: Clock Frequency & Timing Closure
learningObjective: Understand what determines a processor's maximum clock frequency (f_max) and why clock speed alone stopped scaling exponentially.
technicalDefinition: The oscillation rate f = 1 / T_clk (measured in Hertz / GHz) of the synchronous CLK signal distributed across the silicon die to coordinate sequential state transitions.
engineeringExplanation: Every clock period T_clk must exceed the worst-case critical-path delay through combinational logic plus flip-flop clock-to-Q, setup time, and clock skew. Raising frequency requires shorter logic stages (deeper pipelines) or higher supply voltage V, which drives dynamic power (alpha * C * V^2 * f) sharply upward until hitting thermal limits.
generalVsVendorNote: Simulated clockCycles in TIANEDGE reflect deterministic educational stage ticks driven by the user speed slider, distinct from physical GHz silicon timing closure.

title: Instructions Per Cycle (IPC) & Iron Law
learningObjective: Evaluate CPU execution time rigorously using the Iron Law of Processor Performance rather than relying on clock speed alone.
technicalDefinition: Instructions Per Cycle (IPC = 1 / CPI) measures average retired instructions per clock cycle, reflecting microarchitectural efficiency such as superscalar width, out-of-order scheduling, and cache hit rates.
engineeringExplanation: Total program execution time obeys the Iron Law: T_exec = IC * CPI * T_clk = IC / (IPC * f). A processor running at lower frequency f with higher IPC—achieved through wider execution units, accurate branch prediction, and fewer cache misses—frequently outperforms a higher-GHz narrow core.
generalVsVendorNote: TIAN-ISA v1 sequentially retires 1 instruction every 6 cycles (CPI = 6.0, IPC = 0.167) for clear datapath teaching, whereas superscalar hardware retires multiple instructions per cycle (IPC > 1).

title: Parallel Processing Taxonomy
learningObjective: Distinguish Instruction-Level Parallelism (ILP), Data-Level Parallelism (DLP/SIMD), and Thread-Level Parallelism (TLP) across CPU subsystems.
technicalDefinition: Concurrent execution across multiple computation units, vector lanes, or processor cores to boost throughput beyond single-stream scalar execution.
engineeringExplanation: Modern microprocessors exploit multiple parallel tiers simultaneously: ILP (superscalar dispatch across execution units), DLP (SIMD vector units operating on packed data lanes in parallel), and TLP (independent threads across multiple CPU cores). Speedup under parallelization remains bounded by serial program fractions per Amdahl's Law.
generalVsVendorNote: CPU Simulator traces one single instruction stream (SISD educational baseline) inside Core 0, while Chip Anatomy depicts the multi-core and execution-lane architecture.

title: Multi-Core Architecture & Coherence
learningObjective: Explain why microprocessor design pivoted from single high-GHz cores to multi-core CMP dies and how shared caches maintain coherence.
technicalDefinition: Integration of two or more independent processing cores onto a single silicon die (or chiplet package) sharing an on-die interconnect, Last-Level Cache, and memory controller.
engineeringExplanation: Replicating N cores running at moderate frequency and voltage yields vastly superior throughput-per-watt than scaling one core's frequency quadratically in voltage and power. However, replicating private L1 and L2 caches introduces the Cache Coherence Problem: hardware snoop or directory protocols (such as MESI) over the interconnect network ensure two cores never read stale copies of the same memory address.
generalVsVendorNote: Chip Anatomy models a conceptual 4-core symmetric die floorplan; commercial server and desktop CPUs scale from 4 to 128+ cores using ring, mesh, or chiplet interconnects.

title: Power Consumption & Energy Efficiency
learningObjective: Quantify the two components of CMOS processor power (dynamic switching + static leakage) and explain why voltage scaling dominates energy efficiency.
technicalDefinition: Electrical power dissipated by semiconductor switching activity (P_dynamic) and sub-threshold/gate leakage currents (P_static).
engineeringExplanation: Total CMOS power sums switching power P_dyn = alpha * C * V_DD^2 * f and static leakage P_static = I_leak * V_DD. Because dynamic power scales quadratically with supply voltage V_DD, small reductions in V_DD yield massive power savings—motivating Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS) and aggressive clock and power gating across idle core tiles.
generalVsVendorNote: TIANEDGE derives power insights directly from standard CMOS VLSI equations without fabricating proprietary vendor power-telemetry curves.

title: Thermal Management & Heat Dissipation
learningObjective: Trace how microscopic electrical power turns into concentrated silicon heat flux and how CPU packaging mitigates hotspots.
technicalDefinition: The thermal path and control mechanisms (TIM, IHS, external heatsinks, thermal sensors, DVFS throttling) maintaining silicon junction temperature (T_J) within safe reliability limits.
engineeringExplanation: Shrinking transistors concentrates tens or hundreds of watts onto tiny active core regions, creating severe heat density (W/mm^2). Heat conducts from active transistors through bulk silicon and TIM into the copper Integrated Heat Spreader (IHS), governed by thermal resistance T_J = T_A + P * R_theta,JA. Exceeding safe T_J accelerates electromigration and leakage power exponentially, triggering hardware thermal throttling.
generalVsVendorNote: TIANEDGE represents cooling airflow above the IHS conceptually as a visual cue (`C-12` prohibits adding a separate thermal CFD solver).
